reference: The view is passing serializer context, and the hyperlinked fields depend on it. Fully qualified URLs can't be built from the model alone — the serializer needs the current request to know the scheme and host — so hyperlinked relations require the request to be in context. Outside a view you pass it yourself: AccountSerializer(queryset, many=True, context={'request': request}). Context is the general mechanism for handing a serializer anything beyond the object being serialized, and it's readable as self.context from any field logic such as a custom to_representation(). If you genuinely want relative URLs — plausible for an email — you must pass {'request': None} explicitly rather than omitting the key.

user_input: I wrote a handler so every error leaves our API in one consistent envelope, and now the front-end can't tell which field was rejected any more — invalid submissions used to come back keyed by field name and now they arrive as one flat string. What was producing that per-field structure before, and what do I have to keep in my own handler to get it back?
reference: The per-field structure came from the default exception handler, and you replaced it. The chain is: generic views call is_valid(raise_exception=True), which turns a failed validation into a raised ValidationError; the framework's exception handler catches that and renders it as the field-keyed 400 body your front-end was parsing. Your custom handler is wired in through the EXCEPTION_HANDLER setting and takes (exc, context), and it must either return a Response or return None to re-raise — returning your own freshly built Response discards that rendering. The documented pattern is to call REST framework's own exception_handler first to get the standard error response, then decorate what it returned (e.g. adding to response.data) rather than constructing a replacement. Because generic views use raise_exception=True, fixing the handler this way changes validation error style globally across the API.
reference_contexts: The function must take a pair of arguments, the first is the exception to be handled, and the second is a dictionary containing any extra context such as the view currently being handled. The exception handler function should either return a Response object, or return None if the exception cannot be handled.

from rest_framework.views import exception_handler def custom_exception_handler(exc, context): # Call REST framework's default exception handler first, to get the standard error response. response = exception_handler(exc, context)
The exception handler must also be configured in your settings, using the EXCEPTION_HANDLER setting key.
The generic views use the raise_exception=True flag, which means that you can override the style of validation error responses globally in your API. To do so, use a custom exception handler.
llm_response:
The per-field structure was produced by the default `rest_framework.views.exception_handler`.

To restore the per-field structure in your custom handler, you must ensure that when handling validation errors, you include the error details as they are provided by the exception. According to the documentation, while error details are typically simple items, during validation errors they may appear as dictionaries (keyed by field name) or lists.

To get this structure back, your custom handler must:
1.  Check if the exception is a validation error (which the framework handles by raising `ValidationFailed` or similar exceptions where `.detail` contains the error information).
2.  Ensure that your handler preserves the dictionary structure of the `.detail` attribute when it represents field-specific errors, rather than flattening it into a single string. 

You can access the error details using the `.detail` attribute of the exception object passed to your `exception_handler(exc, context)` function.

#### Customizing error responses.¶ {#customizing-error-responses}

The generic views now raise
`ValidationFailed`
exception for invalid data. This exception is then dealt with by the exception handler, rather than the view returning a
`400 Bad Request`
response directly.

This change means that you can now easily customize the style of error responses across your entire API, without having to modify any of the generic views.

## The metadata API¶ {#the-metadata-api}

Behavior for dealing with
`OPTIONS`
requests was previously built directly into the class-based views. This has now been properly separated out into a Metadata API that allows the same pluggable style as other API policies in REST framework.

This makes it far easier to use a different style for
`OPTIONS`
responses throughout your API, and makes it possible to create third-party metadata policies.

## Serializers as HTML forms¶ {#serializers-as-html-forms}

REST framework 3.0 includes templated HTML form rendering for serializers.

This API should not yet be considered finalized, and will only be promoted to public API for the 3.1 release.

REST framework provides a standard exception handler, but users can implement a custom one to alter response styles. A custom handler can utilize the `context` argument to access information like the current view (`context['view']`). To enable a custom handler, it must be configured in the settings using the `EXCEPTION_HANDLER` key; otherwise, the default handler is used.

Additionally, custom API exceptions can be created by inheriting from `APIException`. To inspect these exceptions, three primary attributes and methods are available: `.detail` for the textual error description, `.get_codes()` for the error's code identifier, and `.get_full_details()` for both. While error details are typically simple items, they may appear as lists or dictionaries during validation errors.

The provided text outlines authentication and error handling in the Django REST framework. Unauthenticated requests denied permission return either an HTTP 401 Unauthorized (which requires a `WWW-Authenticate` header) or an HTTP 403 Permission Denied. If a request is authenticated but still lacks permission, a 403 response is always used.

Supported authentication schemes include `BasicAuthentication`, `TokenAuthentication`, and `RemoteUserAuthentication`. Custom schemes can be created by subclassing `BaseAuthentication`. For Django 5.1+, DRF views opt-out of `LoginRequiredMiddleware` to avoid inappropriate redirects, relying instead on `DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES` and `DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`.

Key exceptions include `NotAuthenticated` (401 or 403), `PermissionDenied` (403), and `NotFound` (404). Additionally, the `APIView` manages authenticators, and the request object provides properties like `.method` and `.content_type` to handle HTTP requests and browser enhancements.

## Unauthorized and Forbidden responses¶ {#unauthorized-and-forbidden-responses}

When an unauthenticated request is denied permission there are two different error codes that may be appropriate.

HTTP 401 Unauthorized (https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec10.html#sec10.4.2)
HTTP 403 Permission Denied (https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec10.html#sec10.4.4)

HTTP 401 responses must always include a
`WWW-Authenticate`
header, that instructs the client how to authenticate.  HTTP 403 responses do not include the
`WWW-Authenticate`
header.

The kind of response that will be used depends on the authentication scheme.  Although multiple authentication schemes may be in use, only one scheme may be used to determine the type of response.
The first authentication class set on the view is used when determining the type of response
.

The provided text outlines authentication and error handling in the Django REST framework. Unauthenticated requests denied permission return either an HTTP 401 Unauthorized (which requires a `WWW-Authenticate` header) or an HTTP 403 Permission Denied. For Django 5.1+, DRF views opt-out of `LoginRequiredMiddleware` to avoid inappropriate redirects, relying instead on `DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES` and `DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`.

## Django 5.1+LoginRequiredMiddleware¶ {#django-51-loginrequiredmiddleware}

If you're running Django 5.1+ and use the
LoginRequiredMiddleware (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/middleware/#django.contrib.auth.middleware.LoginRequiredMiddleware)
, please note that all views from DRF are opted-out of this middleware.  This is because the authentication in DRF is based on authentication and permissions classes, which may be determined after the middleware has been applied.  Additionally, when the request is not authenticated, the middleware redirects the user to the login page, which is not suitable for API requests, where it's preferable to return a 401 status code.

REST framework offers an equivalent mechanism for DRF views via the global settings,
`DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`
and
`DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`
.  They should be changed accordingly if you need to enforce that API requests are logged in.

Permissions are used to grant or deny access for different classes of users to different parts of the API.

The simplest style of permission would be to allow access to any authenticated user, and deny access to any unauthenticated user. This corresponds to the
`IsAuthenticated`
class in REST framework.

A slightly less strict style of permission would be to allow full access to authenticated users, but allow read-only access to unauthenticated users. This corresponds to the
`IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`
class in REST framework.

## How permissions are determined¶ {#how-permissions-are-determined}

Permissions in REST framework are always defined as a list of permission classes.

Before running the main body of the view each permission in the list is checked.
If any permission check fails, an
`exceptions.PermissionDenied`
or
`exceptions.NotAuthenticated`
exception will be raised, and the main body of the view will not run.

When the permission checks fail, either a "403 Forbidden" or a "401 Unauthorized" response will be returned, according to the following rules:

The request was successfully authenticated, but permission was denied.
— An HTTP 403 Forbidden response will be returned.

user_input: We moved a huge, constantly-growing table onto cursor pagination to stop clients seeing the same row twice while they scroll. It fixed that, but our mobile client is now broken in a way I didn't anticipate: it deep-links people straight to page 12 of a result set. Why does this style rule that out, and what is it actually requiring of the data underneath?
reference: The two are the same constraint seen from opposite ends. Cursor pagination requires a unique, unchanging ordering over the result set — typically a creation timestamp — and it encodes the client's position as an opaque cursor relative to that ordering rather than as an index. That requirement is what buys you the consistent view you switched for: the client never sees the same item twice even while other clients insert rows mid-scroll. It is also exactly why page numbers are gone — a cursor names a position in an ordering, so the scheme deliberately does not allow the client to arbitrarily index into the result set. The ordering field needs to be unchanging and unique-or-nearly-unique (millisecond timestamps are the canonical example) and must not be a float, since precision errors give wrong results. You set it via the pagination class's `ordering` attribute, and if you combine it with OrderingFilter you should strongly consider restricting which fields clients may order by. Deep links have to be re-expressed as saved cursors, not page indices.
reference_contexts: Cursor based pagination requires that there is a unique, unchanging ordering of items in the result set. This ordering might typically be a creation timestamp on the records, as this presents a consistent ordering to paginate against.

Provides a consistent pagination view. When used properly CursorPagination ensures that the client will never see the same item twice when paging through records, even when new items are being inserted by other clients during the pagination process.
It also requires that the result set presents a fixed ordering, and does not allow the client to arbitrarily index into the result set.

You can modify the ordering by overriding the 'ordering' attribute on the pagination class, or by using the OrderingFilter filter class together with CursorPagination. When used with OrderingFilter you should strongly consider restricting the fields that the user may order by.
Should not be a float. Precision errors easily lead to incorrect results.
llm_response:
`CursorPagination` rules out deep-linking to specific pages because it only provides forward and reverse controls and does not allow the client to navigate to arbitrary positions [1, 2, 7].

Regarding the data underneath, `CursorPagination` requires a fixed, unique, or nearly unique ordering of items [1, 2, 7]. Specifically, the ordering field must satisfy the following constraints:

*   **Unchanging:** It must be a value that is set only once, upon creation (e.g., a timestamp or slug) [3].
*   **Non-nullable:** It must be a non-nullable value that can be coerced to a string [6].
*   **Indexed:** The field should have a database index [6].
*   **Type constraints:** It should not be a float, as precision errors lead to incorrect results; decimals are preferred [2, 6].

This pagination style only presents forward and reverse controls, and does not allow the client to navigate to arbitrary positions.

Cursor based pagination requires that there is a unique, unchanging ordering of items in the result set. This ordering might typically be a creation timestamp on the records, as this presents a consistent ordering to paginate against.

Cursor based pagination is more complex than other schemes. It also requires that the result set presents a fixed ordering, and does not allow the client to arbitrarily index into the result set. However it does provide the following benefits:

Provides a consistent pagination view. When used properly
`CursorPagination`
ensures that the client will never see the same item twice when paging through records, even when new items are being inserted by other clients during the pagination process.
Supports usage with very large datasets. With extremely large datasets pagination using offset-based pagination styles may become inefficient or unusable. Cursor based pagination schemes instead have fixed-time properties, and do not slow down as the dataset size increases.

#### Details and limitations¶ {#details-and-limitations}

Proper use of cursor based pagination requires a little attention to detail.

The provided text outlines various pagination schemes, focusing heavily on `CursorPagination`. Unlike `PageNumberPagination` and `LimitOffsetPagination`, which use page numbers, `CursorPagination` only provides forward and reverse controls. It is ideal for large or frequently changing datasets because it offers fixed-time properties and prevents duplicate items during pagination.

For proper implementation, the ordering field should be a non-nullable, indexed, unchanging value (like a timestamp or slug) that is unique or nearly unique; floats should be avoided in favor of decimals. The default ordering is `"-created"`, but this can be modified via the `ordering` attribute or `OrderingFilter`.

To create custom pagination, inherit from `BasePagination` and override `paginate_queryset` and `get_paginated_response`. Additionally, HTML controls can be customized or disabled by overriding the `template` attribute. Note that `pagination_serializer_class` and `DEFAULT_PAGINATION_SERIALIZER_CLASS` are no longer valid.

Cursor based pagination schemes instead have fixed-time properties, and do not slow down as the dataset size increases.

#### Details and limitations¶ {#details-and-limitations}

Proper use of cursor based pagination requires a little attention to detail. You'll need to think about what ordering you want the scheme to be applied against. The default is to order by
`"-created"`
. This assumes that
there must be a 'created' timestamp field
on the model instances, and will present a "timeline" style paginated view, with the most recently added items first.

You can modify the ordering by overriding the
`'ordering'`
attribute on the pagination class, or by using the
`OrderingFilter`
filter class together with
`CursorPagination`
. When used with
`OrderingFilter`
you should strongly consider restricting the fields that the user may order by.

Proper usage of cursor pagination should have an ordering field that satisfies the following:

Should be an unchanging value, such as a timestamp, slug, or other field that is only set once, on creation.
Should be unique, or nearly unique. Millisecond precision timestamps are a good example.

There are two built-in display styles. The
`PageNumberPagination`
and
`LimitOffsetPagination`
classes display a list of page numbers with previous and next controls. The
`CursorPagination`
class displays a simpler style that only displays a previous and next control.

### Customizing the controls¶ {#customizing-the-controls}

You can override the templates that render the HTML pagination controls. The two built-in styles are:

`rest_framework/pagination/numbers.html`
`rest_framework/pagination/previous_and_next.html`

Providing a template with either of these paths in a global template directory will override the default rendering for the relevant pagination classes.

Alternatively you can disable HTML pagination controls completely by subclassing on of the existing classes, setting
`template = None`
as an attribute on the class. You'll then need to configure your
`DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS`
settings key to use your custom class as the default pagination style.

#### Low-level API¶ {#low-level-api}

The low-level API for determining if a pagination class should display the controls or not is exposed as a
`display_page_controls`
attribute on the pagination instance.

### LimitOffsetPagination¶ {#limitoffsetpagination}

This pagination style mirrors the syntax used when looking up multiple database records. The client includes both a "limit" and an
"offset" query parameter. The limit indicates the maximum number of items to return, and is equivalent to the
`page_size`
in other styles. The offset indicates the starting position of the query in relation to the complete set of unpaginated items.

Request
:


`GET https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=400`


Response
:


`HTTP200OK{"count":1023,"next":"https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=500","previous":"https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=300","results":[…]}`


#### Setup¶ {#setup_1}

To enable the
`LimitOffsetPagination`
style globally, use the following configuration:


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'rest_framework.pagination.LimitOffsetPagination'}`


Optionally, you may also set a
`PAGE_SIZE`
key.

Should be unique, or nearly unique. Millisecond precision timestamps are a good example. This implementation of cursor pagination uses a smart "position plus offset" style that allows it to properly support not-strictly-unique values as the ordering.
Should be a non-nullable value that can be coerced to a string.
Should not be a float. Precision errors easily lead to incorrect results.
Hint: use decimals instead.
(If you already have a float field and must paginate on that, an
example CursorPagination subclass that uses decimals to limit precision is available here (https://gist.github.com/keturn/8bc88525a183fd41c73ffb729b8865be#file-fpcursorpagination-py)
.)
The field should have a database index.

Using an ordering field that does not satisfy these constraints will generally still work, but you'll be losing some of the benefits of cursor pagination.

For more technical details on the implementation we use for cursor pagination, the
"Building cursors for the Disqus API" (https://cra.mr/2011/03/08/building-cursors-for-the-disqus-api)
blog post gives a good overview of the basic approach.

Pagination is performed automatically for viewsets and generic views, while `APIView` requires manual implementation. It can be disabled by setting the pagination class to `None`. Global configuration is managed via `DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS` and `PAGE_SIZE` settings.

Key pagination styles include:
*   **LimitOffsetPagination**: Mirrors database lookups using `limit` (maximum items) and `offset` (starting position) query parameters. It can be configured globally or per-view. Customization options include `default_limit`, `limit_query_param`, `offset_query_param`, and `max_limit`.
*   **CursorPagination**: Uses an opaque "cursor" for forward and reverse navigation, requiring a unique, unchanging ordering of items and prohibiting navigation to arbitrary positions.

Additionally, pagination controls in the browsable API can be customized or disabled using the `template` attribute.

user_input: We run three application servers behind a load balancer and a client on a 100/day allowance managed roughly 300 before anything stopped it — almost exactly three times what it should be. Each server has its own local in-process cache. I think I know what's happening, but I need to understand where the counting actually lives: what does a throttle count against, and how do I move that somewhere all three servers can see?
reference: Your read is right, and the two halves are one story. Throttles are counters held in the cache, keyed per client — for a scoped throttle the key is formed by concatenating the request's scope with the unique user id, or with the IP address for unauthenticated clients. With a local per-process cache each server keeps its own independent counter under that key, so each one grants the full allowance and you get roughly N× your configured rate across N servers. Moving the counters to a backend all three share fixes it. Throttles use the 'default' cache unless told otherwise, and the documented way to point them elsewhere is to subclass the throttle and set its `cache` attribute — `class CustomAnonRateThrottle(AnonRateThrottle): cache = caches['alternate']` — then remember to register that subclass in DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES or the view's throttle_classes, since defining it alone changes nothing.
reference_contexts: If you need to use a cache other than 'default', you can do so by creating a custom throttle class and setting the cache attribute.
from django.core.cache import caches class CustomAnonRateThrottle(AnonRateThrottle): cache = caches['alternate']
You'll need to remember to also set your custom throttle class in the 'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES' settings key, or using the throttle_classes view attribute.
The unique throttle key will then be formed by concatenating the "scope" of the request with the unique user id or IP address.
llm_response:
REST framework throttling counts against Django's cache backend. By default, this uses the `LocMemCache` backend, which is local to each individual server process. This explains why your three servers are each maintaining their own independent count, resulting in the tripled allowance you observed.

To move the throttle count to a location all three servers can see, you must configure a shared cache backend in your Django settings (such as Redis or Memcached) instead of the default `LocMemCache`. 

Once you have configured a shared cache in your Django `CACHES` setting, you can ensure your throttles use it by:

1.  **Using the default:** If you set your shared cache as the `'default'` cache in Django's `CACHES` setting, the built-in throttle classes will automatically use it.
2.  **Using a specific cache:** If you need to use a cache other than `'default'`, you must create a custom throttle class and set the `cache` attribute to point to your shared cache:

```python
from django.core.cache import caches
from rest_framework.throttling import AnonRateThrottle

class CustomAnonRateThrottle(AnonRateThrottle):
    cache = caches['your_shared_cache_name']
```

After creating a custom class, you must register it by setting it in the `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES` setting or by using the `throttle_classes` view attribute.
llm_references:
REST framework throttling uses Django's cache backend, with `LocMemCache` as the default. Custom caches can be implemented by creating a throttle class and setting the `cache` attribute. Built-in implementations are subject to race conditions under high concurrency.

Clients are identified via the `X-Forwarded-For` header or the `REMOTE_ADDR` WSGI variable. The `NUM_PROXIES` setting can be used to strictly identify IPs behind application proxies, though clients behind a unique NAT'd gateway will be treated as one.

Two primary throttle classes are provided: `AnonRateThrottle` for unauthenticated users (based on IP) and `UserRateThrottle` for users (based on user ID, falling back to IP). Throttling can be applied to function-based views using the `@api_view` and `@throttle_classes` decorators, or to routes created with the `@action` decorator, which overrides viewset-level settings.

Multiple throttles can also be used if you want to impose both burst throttling rates, and sustained throttling rates.  For example, you might want to limit a user to a maximum of 60 requests per minute, and 1000 requests per day.

Throttles do not necessarily only refer to rate-limiting requests.  For example a storage service might also need to throttle against bandwidth, and a paid data service might want to throttle against a certain number of a records being accessed.

The application-level throttling that REST framework provides should not be considered a security measure or protection against brute forcing or denial-of-service attacks. Deliberately malicious actors will always be able to spoof IP origins. In addition to this, the built-in throttling implementations are implemented using Django's cache framework, and use non-atomic operations to determine the request rate, which may sometimes result in some fuzziness.

The application-level throttling provided by REST framework is intended for implementing policies such as different business tiers and basic protections against service over-use.

## How throttling is determined¶ {#how-throttling-is-determined}

As with permissions and authentication, throttling in REST framework is always defined as a list of classes.

It is important to understand that if you configure the
`NUM_PROXIES`
setting, then all clients behind a unique
NAT'd (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_address_translation)
gateway will be treated as a single client.

Further context on how the
`X-Forwarded-For`
header works, and identifying a remote client IP can be
found here (http://oxpedia.org/wiki/index.php?title=AppSuite:Grizzly#Multiple_Proxies_in_front_of_the_cluster)
.

The throttle classes provided by REST framework use Django's cache backend.  You should make sure that you've set appropriate
cache settings (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/settings/#caches)
.  The default value of
`LocMemCache`
backend should be okay for simple setups.  See Django's
cache documentation (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/topics/cache/#setting-up-the-cache)
for more details.

`'default'`

`cache`

You'll need to remember to also set your custom throttle class in the

## A note on concurrency¶ {#a-note-on-concurrency}

The built-in throttle implementations are open to
race conditions (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_condition#Data_race)

If your project relies on guaranteeing the number of requests during concurrent requests, you will need to implement your own throttle class. See

`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES':['rest_framework.throttling.ScopedRateThrottle',],'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES':{'contacts':'1000/day','uploads':'20/day'}}`

`ContactListView`
or
`ContactDetailView`

## Custom throttles¶ {#custom-throttles}

To create a custom throttle, override
`BaseThrottle`

`.allow_request(self, request, view)`

`False`

`.wait()`

should return a recommended number of seconds to wait before attempting the next request, or
`None`
.  The
`.wait()`
method will only be called if
`.allow_request()`
has previously returned
`False`

If the
`.wait()`
method is implemented and the request is throttled, then a
`Retry-After`
header will be included in the response.

## How throttling is determined¶ {#how-throttling-is-determined}

As with permissions and authentication, throttling in REST framework is always defined as a list of classes.

Before running the main body of the view each throttle in the list is checked.
If any throttle check fails an
`exceptions.Throttled`
exception will be raised, and the main body of the view will not run.

## Setting the throttling policy¶ {#setting-the-throttling-policy}

The default throttling policy may be set globally, using the
`DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES`
and
`DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES`
settings.  For example.


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES':['rest_framework.throttling.AnonRateThrottle','rest_framework.throttling.UserRateThrottle'],'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES':{'anon':'100/day','user':'1000/day'}}`

Throttling in Django REST framework controls the rate of client requests to an API and is defined as a list of classes. It is intended for implementing business tiers and preventing service over-use, rather than as a security measure against DoS attacks or brute forcing.

Throttling policies can be set globally via `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES` and `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES`, or on a per-view basis. Rates are specified using periods of seconds, minutes, hours, or days. 

Key implementations include `UserRateThrottle` for global per-user restrictions and `ScopedRateThrottle` for restricting specific API parts using a `.throttle_scope` property. Multiple throttles can be combined to manage both burst and sustained rates. To create custom throttles, developers override `BaseThrottle` and implement `.allow_request()`, with an optional `.wait()` method to provide a `Retry-After` response header.

user_input: I hung a custom action off one of our viewsets. It routes fine and I can call it, but two things aren't behaving: the object-level permission I attached to it never seems to be consulted, and after I changed the URL segment to be hyphenated instead of underscored, the link our serializer builds to it started raising NoReverseMatch. How does an action of this kind get its URL and its permissions — are these the same knob or two?
reference: Two knobs, and the URL one is itself two values. The router picks up methods decorated with @action and generates routes for them, with `detail=True` or `detail=False` deciding whether the pattern carries a pk. By default the URL pattern comes from the method name and the URL *name* is the viewset's basename joined to the hyphenated method name — and `url_path` and `url_name` change those two independently. Changing only url_path leaves the reverse name as it was, so a serializer reversing the name you assumed gets NoReverseMatch; set both, or reverse the name that's actually registered. Permissions are separate: @action accepts `permission_classes`, e.g. @action(detail=True, methods=['post'], permission_classes=[IsAdminOrIsSelf]). Two things stop those from firing. Object-level checks only run when the object is fetched through get_object(), so an action that queries the model directly never triggers them — call self.check_object_permissions() yourself if you do. And do not wire an @action method up with .as_view(): that bypasses router setup and may ignore action settings including permission_classes, which is the usual cause of a permission that appears to be attached but never runs.
reference_contexts: If you have ad-hoc methods that should be routable, you can mark them as such with the @action decorator. Like regular actions, extra actions may be intended for either a single object, or an entire collection. To indicate this, set the detail argument to True or False. The router will configure its URL patterns accordingly.

By default, the URL pattern is based on the method name, and the URL name is the combination of the ViewSet.basename and the hyphenated method name. If you don't want to use the defaults for either of these values, you can instead provide the url_path and url_name arguments to the @action decorator.
@action(detail=True, methods=['post'], permission_classes=[IsAdminOrIsSelf]) def set_password(self, request, pk=None): ...
Do not use .as_view() with @action methods. It bypasses router setup and may ignore action settings like permission_classes. Use DefaultRouter for actions.
llm_response:
These are two separate knobs.

### Permissions
The `@action` decorator enables you to override viewset-level configurations, including `permission_classes`. To ensure your object-level permissions are consulted, you must explicitly define the `permission_classes` argument within the `@action` decorator on your method.

### URL Routing and `NoReverseMatch`
The URL name for an extra action is generated by combining the `ViewSet.basename` with the action's `url_name`. By default, the `url_name` is the method name. When you change the URL segment (the `url_path`), you do not automatically change the URL name used for reversing.

If you have changed the URL segment and are now encountering `NoReverseMatch`, it is because the name used in your serializer's link generation no longer matches the expected pattern. You must explicitly set the `url_name` argument in the `@action` decorator to match the name your serializer is attempting to reverse.

**Summary of configuration:**
*   **Permissions:** Use the `permission_classes` argument in the `@action` decorator.
*   **URL Path:** Use the `url_path` argument in the `@action` decorator to define the URL segment.
*   **URL Name:** Use the `url_name` argument in the `@action` decorator to define the name used for reversing.

Example:
```python
@action(methods=['post'], detail=True, url_path='hyphenated-path', url_name='custom-name', permission_classes=[YourPermissionClass])
def your_method(self, request, pk=None):
```

### Routing for extra actions¶ {#routing-for-extra-actions}

A viewset may
mark extra actions for routing (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/viewsets/#marking-extra-actions-for-routing)
by decorating a method with the
`@action`
decorator. These extra actions will be included in the generated routes. For example, given the
`set_password`
method on the
`UserViewSet`
class:


`frommyapp.permissionsimportIsAdminOrIsSelffromrest_framework.decoratorsimportactionclassUserViewSet(ModelViewSet):...@action(methods=['post'],detail=True,permission_classes=[IsAdminOrIsSelf])defset_password(self,request,pk=None):...`

The `@action` decorator allows ViewSets to define custom routable methods beyond standard CRUD operations. By setting the `detail` argument to `True` or `False`, developers specify if the action targets a single object (including `pk` in the URL) or an entire collection. While these actions default to `GET` requests, the `methods` argument can specify other HTTP methods.

The decorator also enables overriding viewset-level configurations like `permission_classes` and `serializer_class`. URL segments and reverse names can be customized using `url_path` and `url_name`. To retrieve all extra actions, use `.get_extra_actions()`, and to obtain an action's URL, use `.reverse_action()`.

Additionally, `SimpleRouter` appends trailing slashes by default, though this can be disabled via the `trailing_slash=False` argument. Note that the `action` attribute is unavailable in `get_parsers`, `get_authenticators`, and `get_content_negotiator` due to the framework lifecycle.

Django REST framework's `ViewSet` classes group related view logic into a single class, promoting consistency and reducing repetition. While `ModelViewSet` and `ReadOnlyModelViewSet` provide standard CRUD operations, the `@action` decorator allows for custom routable methods. These actions can be configured for single objects or collections and can override viewset-level settings like `permission_classes`.

`Router` classes, such as `SimpleRouter` and `DefaultRouter`, automatically generate URL configurations via the `register()` method, which requires a `prefix` and `viewset`. `DefaultRouter` further adds an API root view and `.json` format suffixes. Developers can customize routing using `url_path`, `url_name`, and `lookup_field`, or by subclassing `BaseRouter`. Third-party packages like `drf-nested-routers` extend these capabilities. For maximum control, developers may use regular class-based views instead of viewsets and routers.

Django REST framework provides automatic URL routing to simplify wiring view logic to URLs, similar to functionality found in frameworks like Rails. Instead of manually designing a URL conf, developers can use `Router` classes (such as `SimpleRouter` or `DefaultRouter`) to automatically determine the mapping for `ViewSet` classes.

To implement this, viewsets are registered with a router using the `register()` method, which requires a URL prefix (e.g., `r'users'`) and the corresponding viewset. It is important not to include a trailing slash in the prefix, as routers append them automatically. 

For a complete setup, `rest_framework` must be added to `INSTALLED_APPS`. The resulting `router.urls` are then included in the project's `urlpatterns`. This approach allows for a consistent and quick way to declare common routes for resourceful controllers in a single line of code.

The `ModelSerializer` class does not support nested writable fields by default [1]. Because you have not defined an explicit `.create()` method in your `UserSerializer`, the nested `profile` data is ignored during the save process, which is why the user is created but the profile is not [1, 5].

To fix this, you must override the `.create()` method in your `UserSerializer` to handle the nested data manually [1, 5]:

```python
class UserSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    profile = ProfileSerializer()

    class Meta:
        model = User
        fields = ['username', 'email', 'profile']

    def create(self, validated_data):
        profile_data = validated_data.pop('profile')
        user = User.objects.create(**validated_data)
        Profile.objects.create(user=user, **profile_data)
        return user
```

By popping the `profile` data from `validated_data` and explicitly creating the `Profile` instance associated with the newly created `User`, you enable the support for writable nested representations [1, 5].

If a request is authenticated but still lacks permission, a 403 response is always used.

Supported authentication schemes include `BasicAuthentication`, `TokenAuthentication`, and `RemoteUserAuthentication`. Custom schemes can be created by subclassing `BaseAuthentication`. For Django 5.1+, DRF views opt-out of `LoginRequiredMiddleware` to avoid inappropriate redirects, relying instead on `DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES` and `DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`.

Key exceptions include `NotAuthenticated` (401 or 403), `PermissionDenied` (403), and `NotFound` (404). Additionally, the `APIView` manages authenticators, and the request object provides properties like `.method` and `.content_type` to handle HTTP requests and browser enhancements.

## Object level permissions¶ {#object-level-permissions}

REST framework permissions also support object-level permissioning.  Object level permissions are used to determine if a user should be allowed to act on a particular object, which will typically be a model instance.

Object level permissions are run by REST framework's generic views when
`.get_object()`
is called.
As with view level permissions, an
`exceptions.PermissionDenied`
exception will be raised if the user is not allowed to act on the given object.

Your `has_object_permission` method is not being called because you are using a custom `APIView`. Unlike generic views, custom views do not automatically trigger object-level permission checks.

To fix this, you must explicitly call `self.check_object_permissions(request, obj)` in your view after you have retrieved the object instance.

Update your `NoteDetail` view as follows:

```python
class NoteDetail(APIView):
    permission_classes = [IsOwner]

    def get(self, request, pk):
        note = Note.objects.get(pk=pk)
        # Explicitly check object permissions
        self.check_object_permissions(request, note)
        return Response(NoteSerializer(note).data)
```

This method will raise a `PermissionDenied` or `NotAuthenticated` exception if the permission check fails, or simply return if the user is permitted to view the object.

## Setting the permission policy¶ {#setting-the-permission-policy}

The default permission policy may be set globally, using the
`DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`
setting.  For example.


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES':['rest_framework.permissions.IsAuthenticated',]}`


If not specified, this setting defaults to allowing unrestricted access:


`'DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES':['rest_framework.permissions.AllowAny',]`


You can also set the authentication policy on a per-view, or per-viewset basis,
using the
`APIView`
class-based views.


`fromrest_framework.permissionsimportIsAuthenticatedfromrest_framework.responseimportResponsefromrest_framework.viewsimportAPIViewclassExampleView(APIView):permission_classes=[IsAuthenticated]defget(self,request,format=None):content={'status':'request was permitted'}returnResponse(content)`

As well as global permissions, that are run against all incoming requests, you can also create object-level permissions, that are only run against operations that affect a particular object instance.  For example:


`classIsOwnerOrReadOnly(permissions.BasePermission):"""
Object-level permission to only allow owners of an object to edit it.
Assumes the model instance has an `owner` attribute.
"""defhas_object_permission(self,request,view,obj):# Read permissions are allowed to any request,# so we'll always allow GET, HEAD or OPTIONS requests.ifrequest.methodinpermissions.SAFE_METHODS:returnTrue# Instance must have an attribute named `owner`.returnobj.owner==request.user`

`self.check_object_permissions(request, obj)`
from the view once you have the object instance.  This call will raise an appropriate
`APIException`
if any object-level permission checks fail, and will otherwise simply return.

reference_contexts: For performance reasons the generic views will not automatically apply object level permissions to each instance in a queryset when returning a list of objects.
Often when you're using object level permissions you'll also want to filter the queryset appropriately, to ensure that users only have visibility onto instances that they are permitted to view.
The simplest way to filter the queryset of any view that subclasses GenericAPIView is to override the .get_queryset() method.
llm_response:
Object-level permissions, such as those implemented in `has_object_permission()`, are only applied to retrieve, modify, and deletion actions. They are not automatically applied to list views because generic views only check object-level permissions for views that retrieve a single model instance. Consequently, permission checks for list actions are applied to the entire object type rather than individual instances.

To scope a list response, you must filter the `queryset` separately. You should override the `get_queryset()` method in your view to restrict the objects returned from the database.

**Recommended approach:**
Override `get_queryset()` to filter by the currently authenticated user:

```python
def get_queryset(self):
    user = self.request.user
    return Purchase.objects.filter(purchaser=user)
```

Alternatively, if you need to filter based on a URL parameter, you can access the URL kwargs:

```python
def get_queryset(self):
    username = self.kwargs['username']
    return Purchase.objects.filter(purchaser__username=username)
```

Permissions in Django REST framework determine if a request is granted or denied access, working alongside authentication and throttling. Checks occur at the start of a view using `request.user` and `request.auth`. Permissions are defined as a list of classes; if any fail, the view body does not run, resulting in either a "403 Forbidden" or "401 Unauthorized" response.

Key permission classes include:
* `AllowAny`: Unrestricted access.
* `IsAuthenticated`: Only registered users.
* `IsAdminUser`: Only users where `user.is_staff` is True.
* `IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`: Full access for authenticated users; read-only access (`GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`) for unauthenticated users.

Additionally, object-level permissions determine if a user can act on a specific model instance during `.get_object()` calls. Permission composition is supported using `&` (and), `|` (or), and `~` (not) operators with standard logical precedence.

The provided text outlines permission management in Django REST Framework. Global policies are set via `DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES` or on a per-view basis using `permission_classes`. 

Object-level permissions apply to specific instances. While generic views handle these by default, custom views must explicitly call `.check_object_permissions(request, obj)`, which raises `PermissionDenied` or `NotAuthenticated` upon failure. Most provided permission classes, except `DjangoObjectPermissions`, require subclassing and implementing `has_object_permission()` for object-level checks.

Key limitations include:
* Generic views do not automatically apply object-level permissions to querysets in list views.
* Object-level permissions are not applied during object creation because `get_object()` is not called; restrictions must instead be implemented in the Serializer or `perform_create()` method.

Additionally, `SAFE_METHODS` ('GET', 'OPTIONS', 'HEAD') can be used to distinguish between read and write operations.

To fix the issue where your mobile client receives relative URLs instead of fully qualified ones, you must include the current `request` in the serializer context when instantiating the serializer in your view.

Update your `views.py` as follows:

```python
class AccountList(APIView):
    def get(self, request):
        accounts = Account.objects.all()
        # Pass the request in the context
        data = AccountSerializer(accounts, many=True, context={'request': request}).data
        return Response(data)
```

According to the documentation, including the `request` ensures that hyperlinks can include the appropriate hostname, resulting in fully qualified URLs (e.g., `http://api.example.com/accounts/1/`) rather than relative ones (e.g., `/accounts/1/`).

Regarding your colleague's use of `ListAPIView`, it likely works without extra code because `ListAPIView` (and other generic views) automatically handles the inclusion of the `request` in the serializer context.

### How hyperlinked views are determined¶ {#how-hyperlinked-views-are-determined}

There needs to be a way of determining which views should be used for hyperlinking to model instances.

By default hyperlinks are expected to correspond to a view name that matches the style
`'{model_name}-detail'`
, and looks up the instance by a
`pk`
keyword argument.

### Inspecting aModelSerializer¶ {#inspecting-a-modelserializer}

Serializer classes generate helpful verbose representation strings, that allow you to fully inspect the state of their fields. This is particularly useful when working with
`ModelSerializers`
where you want to determine what set of fields and validators are being automatically created for you.

To do so, open the Django shell, using
`python manage.py shell`
, then import the serializer class, instantiate it, and print the object representation…

Or we can get a particular snippet by referencing its id:


`httpGEThttp://127.0.0.1:8000/snippets/2/--unsortedHTTP/1.1200OK...{"id":2,"title":"","code":"print(\"hello, world\")\n","linenos":false,"language":"python","style":"friendly"}`

## Where are we now¶ {#where-are-we-now}

We're doing okay so far, we've got a serialization API that feels pretty similar to Django's Forms API, and some regular Django views.

Our API views don't do anything particularly special at the moment, beyond serving
`json`
responses, and there are some error handling edge cases we'd still like to clean up, but it's a functioning Web API.

We'll see how we can start to improve things in
part 2 of the tutorial (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/tutorial/2-requests-and-responses/)
.

For more information, see the
custom pagination styles (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/pagination/#custom-pagination-styles)
documentation.

The global pagination settings are not reaching your view because you are using a regular `APIView`. Pagination is only performed automatically when using generic views or viewsets.

To fix this, you must manually implement the pagination API within your `APIView`. You need to:

1.  Instantiate your pagination class (e.g., `PageNumberPagination`).
2.  Call `paginate_queryset(queryset, request, view=self)` to split the result set.
3.  Return the result using `get_paginated_response(data)`.

**Example implementation:**

```python
from rest_framework.pagination import PageNumberPagination
from rest_framework.views import APIView
from rest_framework.response import Response

class NoteList(APIView):
    def get(self, request):
        notes = Note.objects.all()
        
        # 1. Instantiate the pagination class
        paginator = PageNumberPagination()
        
        # 2. Paginate the queryset
        result_page = paginator.paginate_queryset(notes, request)
        
        # 3. Serialize the paginated data and return the response
        serializer = NoteSerializer(result_page, many=True)
        return paginator.get_paginated_response(serializer.data)
```

For further reference on how to implement this, you should consult the source code for `mixins.ListModelMixin` and `generics.GenericAPIView`.

## Setting the pagination style¶ {#setting-the-pagination-style}

The pagination style may be set globally, using the
`DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS`
and
`PAGE_SIZE`
setting keys. For example, to use the built-in limit/offset pagination, you would do something like this:


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'rest_framework.pagination.LimitOffsetPagination','PAGE_SIZE':100}`

Django REST framework provides customizable pagination to split large result sets into pages, functioning automatically for generic views and viewsets but requiring manual implementation in `APIView`. Configuration is managed globally via `REST_FRAMEWORK` settings (`DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS`, `PAGE_SIZE`) or per-view using `pagination_class`.

Three primary styles are available:
*   **PageNumberPagination**: Uses page numbers; customizable via `page_query_param` and `page_size`.
*   **LimitOffsetPagination**: Uses `limit` and `offset` parameters.
*   **CursorPagination**: Uses an opaque cursor for forward/reverse navigation, ideal for large, changing datasets; requires a unique, non-nullable, indexed ordering field.

Custom pagination is created by inheriting from `BasePagination` and overriding `paginate_queryset` and `get_paginated_response`. Browsable API controls can be modified via the `template` attribute. Note that `PAGE_SIZE` replaces `PAGINATE_BY`, and several older attributes like `pagination_serializer_class` are no longer valid.

`GET https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=4`


Response
:


`HTTP200OK{"count":1023,"next":"https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=5","previous":"https://api.example.org/accounts/?page=3","results":[…]}`

`PageNumberPagination`
style globally, use the following configuration, and set the
`PAGE_SIZE`

`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'rest_framework.pagination.PageNumberPagination','PAGE_SIZE':100}`


On
`GenericAPIView`
subclasses you may also set the
`pagination_class`
attribute to select
`PageNumberPagination`
on a per-view basis.

attribute.

#### New pagination schemes.¶ {#new-pagination-schemes}

Until now, there has only been a single built-in pagination style in REST framework. We now have page, limit/offset and cursor based schemes included by default.

The cursor based pagination scheme is particularly smart, and is a better approach for clients iterating through large or frequently changing result sets. The scheme supports paging against non-unique indexes, by using both cursor and limit/offset information. It also allows for both forward and reverse cursor pagination. this blog post (https://cra.mr/2011/03/08/building-cursors-for-the-disqus-api)
on the subject.

### LimitOffsetPagination¶ {#limitoffsetpagination}

This pagination style mirrors the syntax used when looking up multiple database records. The client includes both a "limit" and an
"offset" query parameter. The limit indicates the maximum number of items to return, and is equivalent to the
`page_size`
in other styles. The offset indicates the starting position of the query in relation to the complete set of unpaginated items.

Request
:


`GET https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=400`


Response
:


`HTTP200OK{"count":1023,"next":"https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=500","previous":"https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=300","results":[…]}`


#### Setup¶ {#setup_1}

To enable the
`LimitOffsetPagination`
style globally, use the following configuration:


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'rest_framework.pagination.LimitOffsetPagination'}`


Optionally, you may also set a
`PAGE_SIZE`
key.

That object contains only the data in the requested page.
The
`get_paginated_response`
method is passed to the serialized page data and should return a
`Response`
instance.

Note that the
`paginate_queryset`
method may set state on the pagination instance, that may later be used by the
`get_paginated_response`
method.

### Example¶ {#example}

Suppose we want to replace the default pagination output style with a modified format that includes the next and previous links under in a nested 'links' key. We could specify a custom pagination class like so:


`classCustomPagination(pagination.PageNumberPagination):defget_paginated_response(self,data):returnResponse({'links':{'next':self.get_next_link(),'previous':self.get_previous_link()},'count':self.page.paginator.count,'results':data})`


We'd then need to set up the custom class in our configuration:


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'my_project.apps.core.pagination.CustomPagination','PAGE_SIZE':100}`

To accept raw file uploads, you must use the `FileUploadParser` in your view. This parser is designed for native clients that upload files as raw data requests.

### Implementation
1. **Update your view**: Add `parser_classes = [FileUploadParser]` to your `UploadView`. Because `FileUploadParser` matches any content type, it should generally be the only parser set on the view.
2. **Handle the filename**: Since you are using a `filename` URL keyword argument in your path, `FileUploadParser` will automatically use that argument as the filename for the uploaded file.

**Updated `views.py`:**
```python
from rest_framework.parsers import FileUploadParser
from rest_framework.views import APIView
from rest_framework.response import Response

class UploadView(APIView):
    parser_classes = [FileUploadParser]

    def put(self, request, filename):
        file_obj = request.data['file']
        # save(file_obj, filename)
        return Response(status=204)
```

### Why this works
* **415 Error**: The 415 Unsupported Media Type error occurs because your current configuration is likely using default parsers that do not support raw binary streams. `FileUploadParser` is specifically built to handle raw file upload content.
* **Filename**: When a `filename` URL keyword argument is provided (as in your `urls.py`), the `FileUploadParser` uses that value as the filename. If you did not provide it in the URL, you would be required to set the filename in the `Content-Disposition` HTTP header (e.g., `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=upload.jpg`).
* **Streaming**: `FileUploadParser` respects Django's standard `FILE_UPLOAD_HANDLERS` setting and the `request.upload_handlers` attribute, which allows for the handling of large file uploads.

## Request parsing¶ {#request-parsing}

REST framework's Request objects provide flexible request parsing that allows you to treat requests with JSON data or other media types in the same way that you would normally deal with form data.

### .data¶ {#data}

`request.data`
returns the parsed content of the request body.  This is similar to the standard
`request.POST`
and
`request.FILES`
attributes except that:

It includes all parsed content, including
file and non-file
inputs.
It supports parsing the content of HTTP methods other than
`POST`
, meaning that you can access the content of
`PUT`
and
`PATCH`
requests.
It supports REST framework's flexible request parsing, rather than just supporting form data.  For example you can handle incoming
JSON data (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/parsers/#jsonparser)
similarly to how you handle incoming
form data (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/parsers/#formparser)
.

:
`multipart/form-data`

### FileUploadParser¶ {#fileuploadparser}

Parses raw file upload content.  The
`request.data`
property will be a dictionary with a single key
`'file'`
containing the uploaded file.

If the view used with
`FileUploadParser`
is called with a
`filename`
URL keyword argument, then that argument will be used as the filename.

If it is called without a
`filename`
URL keyword argument, then the client must set the filename in the
`Content-Disposition`

`Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=upload.jpg`
.

.media_type
:
`*/*`

The
`FileUploadParser`
is for usage with native clients that can upload the file as a raw data request.  For web-based uploads, or for native clients with multipart upload support, you should use the
`MultiPartParser`

Django REST framework provides a `Request` object with a `request.data` attribute that handles arbitrary data for POST, PUT, and PATCH methods, and a `Response` object that uses content negotiation to determine the return content type. 

Content types can be controlled via the `Content-Type` header, `Accept` header, or URL format suffixes. The `URL_FORMAT_OVERRIDE` setting (defaulting to `'format'`) allows overriding the `Accept` header via query parameters.

For testing, `APIRequestFactory` simplifies request creation; methods like `post`, `put`, and `patch` include a `format` argument (defaulting to `'multipart'`, with `'json'` also available) or a `content_type` flag for explicit encoding.

Additionally, the browsable API uses the `ajax-form` library to support browser-based PUT, DELETE, and non-form content (like JSON) via `data-method` and `data-override` attributes, as HTML5 does not natively support PUT and DELETE forms.

Django REST framework provides built-in Parser classes to handle various media types, allowing `request.data` to treat JSON, form data, and files consistently across different HTTP methods like POST, PUT, and PATCH. The framework determines the appropriate parser by examining the request's `Content-Type` header.

Key built-in parsers include:
* **JSONParser**: For `application/json`.
* **FormParser** and **MultiPartParser**: For HTML form data and file uploads.
* **FileUploadParser**: For raw file uploads (typically used alone as its media type matches any content type).

Parsers can be configured globally via `DEFAULT_PARSER_CLASSES` or per view using `APIView`. Developers can also create custom parsers by overriding `BaseParser`. Additionally, the `Request` object extends Django's `HttpRequest`, providing `.data` for parsed content and `.stream` for the raw request body.

The simplest way to filter the queryset of any view that subclasses

`.get_queryset()`
method.

Overriding this method allows you to customize the queryset returned by the view in a number of different ways.

Django REST framework's generic list views return an entire queryset by default, but this can be restricted by overriding the `.get_queryset()` method. This allows for dynamic behavior, such as filtering results based on the currently authenticated user via `request.user`. 

To improve performance and avoid N+1 query patterns when serializers access related objects, `.get_queryset()` or the `queryset` attribute can be optimized using `select_related()` for ForeignKey and OneToOneField relationships, and `prefetch_related()` for reverse or many-to-many relationships.

Additionally, if a filter backend is configured, it applies to both list views and single object lookups; if filtering conditions are not met for a specific object, a 404 response is returned. For more complex detail view lookups, the `get_object()` method can be overridden. Overridden `.get_queryset()` methods can be used in conjunction with generic filtering.

REST framework supports generic filtering backends to construct complex searches and filters, which can be set globally via `DEFAULT_FILTER_BACKENDS` or on a per-view/viewset basis using `GenericAPIView`. For simple equality-based filtering, the `filterset_fields` attribute can be used, while advanced requirements allow for a custom `FilterSet` class. 

The `SearchFilter` class enables single query parameter searching based on a `search_fields` attribute. Custom filter backends can be created by inheriting from `BaseFilterBackend` and implementing `filter_queryset`. To add an interface to the browsable API, filters should implement a `to_html` method. 

Additionally, several third-party packages extend these capabilities: `django-rest-framework-filters` for relationship filtering, `djangorestframework-word-filter` for full-word searches, and `django-url-filter` and `drf-url-filters` for human-friendly URL filtering and query parameter validation.

llm_response:
To catch the uniqueness constraint violation before it reaches the database, you should use the `UniqueValidator` on the `slug` field in your `BlogPostSerializer`.

The `UniqueValidator` is designed to enforce `unique=True` constraints on model fields when using an explicit `Serializer` class. You apply it by adding it to the `validators` argument of the field definition.

Update your `serializers.py` as follows:

```python
from rest_framework import serializers
from rest_framework.validators import UniqueValidator
from .models import BlogPost

class BlogPostSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    slug = serializers.SlugField(
        max_length=100, 
        validators=[UniqueValidator(queryset=BlogPost.objects.all())]
    )
    title = serializers.CharField(max_length=200)
```

By adding this validator, the serializer's `is_valid()` method will check the uniqueness of the `slug` against the provided queryset and return a field error instead of allowing the save to proceed and trigger a database `IntegrityError`.

The `OrderingFilter` defaults to allowing ordering on any readable field defined in your `serializer_class` if the `ordering_fields` attribute is not explicitly specified on the view.

To constrain the fields that can be used for ordering and prevent the exposure of sensitive model fields like `password`, you must explicitly define the `ordering_fields` attribute on your view.

**Recommended approach:**
Set `ordering_fields` to a list of the specific fields you want to allow:

```python
class UserListView(generics.ListAPIView):
    queryset = User.objects.all()
    serializer_class = UserSerializer
    filter_backends = [filters.OrderingFilter]
    ordering_fields = ['username', 'id'] # Only these fields will be allowed
```

This explicitly restricts the API to only accept the fields provided in the list, preventing attackers from ordering by unauthorized fields.

By overriding `get_object` manually, you bypassed the automatic object-level permission check performed by generic views.

Generic views handle object-level permissions by calling `.check_object_permissions(request, obj)` after retrieving the object.     self.check_object_permissions(self.request, obj)

## A note on concurrency¶ {#a-note-on-concurrency}

The built-in throttle implementations are open to
race conditions (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_condition#Data_race)
, so under high concurrency they may allow a few extra requests through.

If your project relies on guaranteeing the number of requests during concurrent requests, you will need to implement your own throttle class. See
issue #5181 (https://github.com/encode/django-rest-framework/issues/5181)
for more details.

Throttling in Django REST framework controls the rate of client requests to an API and is defined as a list of classes. It is intended for implementing business tiers and preventing service over-use, rather than as a security measure against DoS attacks or brute forcing.

Throttling policies can be set globally via `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES` and `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES`, or on a per-view basis. Rates are specified using periods of seconds, minutes, hours, or days. 

Key implementations include `UserRateThrottle` for global per-user restrictions and `ScopedRateThrottle` for restricting specific API parts using a `.throttle_scope` property. Multiple throttles can be combined to manage both burst and sustained rates. To create custom throttles, developers override `BaseThrottle` and implement `.allow_request()`, with an optional `.wait()` method to provide a `Retry-After` response header.

The provided text outlines authentication and error handling in the Django REST framework. Unauthenticated requests denied permission return either an HTTP 401 Unauthorized (which requires a `WWW-Authenticate` header) or an HTTP 403 Permission Denied. If a request is authenticated but still lacks permission, a 403 response is always used.

Supported authentication schemes include `BasicAuthentication`, `TokenAuthentication`, and `RemoteUserAuthentication`. Custom schemes can be created by subclassing `BaseAuthentication`. For Django 5.1+, DRF views opt-out of `LoginRequiredMiddleware` to avoid inappropriate redirects, relying instead on `DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES` and `DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`.

Key exceptions include `NotAuthenticated` (401 or 403), `PermissionDenied` (403), and `NotFound` (404). Additionally, the `APIView` manages authenticators, and the request object provides properties like `.method` and `.content_type` to handle HTTP requests and browser enhancements.

The issue is that you are defining a custom method `filtered()` on your class, but you are not overriding the `get_queryset()` method that the view uses to determine the data it returns. Because `queryset` is defined as a class attribute, it is evaluated once and shared across requests; modifying it or failing to dynamically filter it based on the request leads to the data leakage you are observing.

To fix this, you should override the `get_queryset()` method to ensure the queryset is filtered dynamically for every request based on the authenticated user.

**Recommended approach:**
Override `get_queryset()` to return the filtered results:

```python
class OrderList(generics.ListAPIView):
    serializer_class = OrderSerializer

    def get_queryset(self):
        """
        This view should return a list of all the orders
        for the currently authenticated user.
        """
        user = self.request.user
        return Order.objects.filter(user=user)
```

**Alternative approach:**
You can also use a custom filter backend by overriding `BaseFilterBackend` and the `.filter_queryset(self, request, queryset, view)` method. This is useful if you want to restrict which objects are visible to a user across multiple views:

```python
class IsOwnerFilterBackend(filters.BaseFilterBackend):
    """
    Filter that only allows users to see their own objects.
    """
    def filter_queryset(self, request, queryset, view):
        return queryset.filter(user=request.user)
```

You would then add this backend to your view's `filter_backends` attribute.

This is not a bug. All Django REST Framework (DRF) views are opted-out of `LoginRequiredMiddleware` because DRF authentication and permissions are determined after middleware is applied, and the middleware's redirect behavior is unsuitable for API requests, which should return a 401 status code instead.

To enforce that API requests are logged in, you must use DRF's global settings in your `settings.py` file. You should configure `DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES` within the `REST_FRAMEWORK` dictionary to require authentication.

For example, to require authentication globally for your API, set:

```python
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES': [
        'rest_framework.permissions.IsAuthenticated',
    ]
}
```

This ensures that API requests are restricted to authenticated users, providing the blanket guarantee you require.

Note that if deploying to

.

llm_response:
Calling the view directly via `APIRequestFactory` behaves differently because, unlike Django's standard `RequestFactory`, REST framework performs CSRF validation inside the view. When using `APIRequestFactory`, CSRF validation is disabled by default.

The recommended way to write these tests is to use the **`APIClient`** class instead of `APIRequestFactory`. `APIClient` extends Django's standard `Client` class and is designed to handle the full request/response cycle, including authentication and CSRF validation, more similarly to how a browser interacts with your API.

To use `APIClient`:

1.  **Switch to `APIClient`**: Replace `APIRequestFactory` with `APIClient`.
    ```python
    from rest_framework.test import APIClient
    client = APIClient()
    client.post('/notes/', {'title': 'new idea'}, format='json')
    ```

2.  **Handle Authentication**: Since your view uses `SessionAuthentication`, you must log the client in to satisfy the authentication requirement and trigger CSRF validation:
    ```python
    client.login(username='user', password='password')
    ```

3.  **Alternative (API Test Cases)**: You can also use `APITestCase`, which provides a pre-configured `self.client` (an instance of `APIClient`) that mirrors Django's test case classes:
    ```python
    from rest_framework.test import APITestCase

    class NoteTests(APITestCase):
        def test_create_note(self):
            self.client.login(...)
            response = self.client.post('/notes/', {'title': 'x'}, format='json')
    ```

If you must continue using `APIRequestFactory` for direct view testing, you can explicitly enable CSRF validation by setting the `enforce_csrf_checks` flag when instantiating the factory:
```python
factory = APIRequestFactory(enforce_csrf_checks=True)
```
Note that CSRF validation will only apply to session-authenticated views.

When using REST framework, CSRF validation takes place inside the view, so the request factory needs to disable view-level CSRF checks.

Extends
Django's existing Client class (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/topics/testing/tools/#the-test-client)
.

### Making requests¶ {#making-requests}

The
`APIClient`
class supports the same request interface as Django's standard
`Client`
class.  This means that the standard
`.get()`
,
`.post()`
,
`.put()`
,
`.patch()`
,
`.delete()`
,
`.head()`
and

methods are all available.  For example:


`fromrest_framework.testimportAPIClientclient=APIClient()client.post('/notes/',{'title':'new idea'},format='json')`

`.token`

response=view(request)`

### Forcing CSRF validation¶ {#forcing-csrf-validation}

By default, requests created with
`APIRequestFactory`

flag when instantiating the factory.

REST framework includes a few helper classes that extend Django's existing test framework, and improve support for making API requests.

## APIRequestFactory¶ {#apirequestfactory}

Extends
Django's existing RequestFactory class (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/topics/testing/advanced/#django.test.client.RequestFactory)
.

### Creating test requests¶ {#creating-test-requests}

The
`APIRequestFactory`
class supports an almost identical API to Django's standard
`RequestFactory`
class.  This means that the standard
`.get()`
,
`.post()`
,
`.put()`
,
`.patch()`
,
`.delete()`
,
`.head()`
and
`.options()`
methods are all available.

Django REST framework provides several tools to enhance Django's testing capabilities. `APIRequestFactory` allows for direct view testing with methods to force authentication and toggle CSRF validation. `APIClient` extends Django's `Client` for API-specific requests, offering `.login()`, `.credentials()`, and `.force_authenticate()` for various authentication schemes. `RequestsClient` enables end-to-end, in-process testing using the `requests` library interface, requiring fully qualified URLs.

The framework includes specialized test case classes like `APITestCase` and `URLPatternsTestCase` to streamline API testing. For response validation, inspecting `response.data` is recommended over parsing `response.content`. Additionally, the provided documentation outlines how to run tests via `./runtests.py` with various flags for output control and specific test targeting, or using `tox` for multi-environment testing. Tests requiring database access should inherit from `django.test.TestCase` or use the `@pytest.mark.django_db()` decorator.

`fromrest_framework.testimportRequestsClientclient=RequestsClient()response=client.get('http://testserver/users/')assertresponse.status_code==200`


Note that the requests client requires you to pass fully qualified URLs.

### RequestsClient and working with the database¶ {#requestsclient-and-working-with-the-database}

The
`RequestsClient`
class is useful if you want to write tests that solely interact with the service interface. This is a little stricter than using the standard Django test client, as it means that all interactions should be via the API.

If you're using
`RequestsClient`
you'll want to ensure that test setup, and results assertions are performed as regular API calls, rather than interacting with the database models directly. For example, rather than checking that
`Customer.objects.count() == 3`
you would list the customers endpoint, and ensure that it contains three records.

### Headers & Authentication¶ {#headers-authentication}

Custom headers and authentication credentials can be provided in the same way
as
when using a standard requests.Session instance (https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user/advanced/#session-objects)
.

`client=APIClient(enforce_csrf_checks=True)`


As usual CSRF validation will only apply to any session authenticated views.  This means CSRF validation will only occur if the client has been logged in by calling
`login()`
.

## RequestsClient¶ {#requestsclient}

REST framework also includes a client for interacting with your application
using the popular Python library,
`requests`
. This may be useful if:

You are expecting to interface with the API primarily from another Python service,
and want to test the service at the same level as the client will see.
You want to write tests in such a way that they can also be run against a staging or
live environment. (See "Live tests" below.)

This exposes exactly the same interface as if you were using a requests session
directly.


`fromrest_framework.testimportRequestsClientclient=RequestsClient()response=client.get('http://testserver/users/')assertresponse.status_code==200`

Doing so may require some careful
attention to setup and teardown to ensure that the tests run in a way that they
do not directly affect customer data.
